title: Which nodes are worth staging
starter:
def stage_set(g: list[tuple[int, list[int]]]) -> list[int]:
    """g is a list of (id, srcs): node id reads the nodes in srcs. A leaf has srcs == [].
    Return, sorted ascending, every non-leaf id with two or more distinct consumers
    (a node read twice by the same consumer is still one use)."""
    return []
hints: First count each node's consumers: for every (id, srcs), id consumes each node in srcs. Loop over set(srcs) so a consumer that reads a node twice counts once.
collections.Counter does the counting. Then keep the ids that have at least 2 distinct consumers and a non-empty srcs of their own (leaves like buffer loads aren't worth staging).
sorted(...) gives ascending order. A Counter returns 0 for a missing key, so nodes nobody reads need no special case.
prompt: A graph is a list of (id, srcs) tuples: node id reads the nodes in the list srcs, and a leaf has srcs == []. Write stage_set(g: list[tuple[int, list[int]]]) -> list[int]: every non-leaf id that has two or more distinct consumers, sorted ascending. A node read twice by the same consumer (like mul %c %c) is still one use, since rangeify builds that element once per index. That's the candidate list a materialization pass starts from. An empty result prints as an empty line.

answer.explain: Counting uses is the first question a materialization pass asks: a value with one consumer can always be fused into it, and a value with two consumers is the candidate for staging. A consumer that reads a node twice (like mul c c) is one use, because hash consing makes rangeify build that element once per index. Leaves are excluded because there is nothing to recompute.
